Mr Johnson.

blocks.text: PROFESSOR OWEN ARTHURS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR JOHNSON
Welcome back, Professor Arthurs. For the sake of the record, would you just identify yourself, please?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm Owen Arthurs, I'm a consultant radiologist at Great Ormond Street Hospital in London.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. Professor Arthurs, you have assisted the court before with evidence about several of the children that are involved in this case. Two of the children in respect of whom you have given evidence are [Baby E] and [Baby D].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the context of the evidence that you previously gave to the jury, you were asked a question or asked questions about the prevalence of air in the great vessels post-mortem and explanations for that.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And you previously referred to a medical paper, I think; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: If you could just remind the jury of the gist of the evidence you gave earlier so that we can put into context what you're about to add to that.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes. So I was asked about how common it was to see post-mortem gas in some of the great vessels of the body, the aorta and the IVC, and I made reference to a paper that I had been the senior author on, on writing back in 2015, which we published. That was a paper that looked at post-mortem CT in a large range of children, several of whom were older children, and so I was asked the question whether any of those were particularly relevant to the babies in this case.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. Just to help us all, because we are not as familiar with this material as you are, or the basis for it, you have mentioned CT there, and in this case we haven't got CT scans or --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: What's the difference between a CT scan and a radiograph or X-ray?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In very simple terms, an X-ray takes one image through the body and so you get a picture of a three-dimensional structure in two dimensions, if you like, a black and white photograph. A CT scanner does that repeatedly around the body and so can create a 3D reconstruction of the body. Many of you will have had a CT scan of the chest or the abdomen, so what we are able to do then with those pictures is look at them in many
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: different ways to find very small aspects of things that you might miss on a simple two-dimensional photograph, if you like.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So does it follow that a CT scan is much more discriminatory, much more detailed than a radiograph?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, often that's true. It involves a higher dose of radiation, you are using lots of different X-rays at the same time, but it tends to give a more detailed picture and a more precise picture in terms of localising things, which why we use it in clinical practice.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So things that may not show up on a traditional X-ray do show up on a CT scan?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's usually the case.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And this was a study that you authored, with others, that related or had as its database CT imagery rather than X-ray imagery?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right because we wanted to know how common -- or where you saw gas at post-mortem -- the purpose of the study wasn't to address this specific question, but we wanted to use the best technique that we had and we have a large collection of CT scans in children who have died. So we wanted to try and categorise, if you like, where those things occurred.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. So it was that when you gave evidence on 21 October last year, his Lordship asked you a direct question:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "How many were babies who were 1 to 2 days old and were premature?"
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Do you remember that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The point being, was the material in the paper directly relevant to the issues or the control sample, the babies, in this case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And I think your response on that occasion was that you couldn't say off the top of your head, but very few, probably none, was the answer you gave previously.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Since then you have gone back to the paper; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In fact, to the raw data. So because we wrote the paper we have all the raw data stored, we have all the scans still there on our database. We have an obligation to keep the information for 10 to 15 years for data governance reasons. So I was able to go back and actually look at the specific cases inn that and actually try and address that question if it would help the court to explain how many of this children were in that period and if none, then so be it.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. And what was the result of your further research?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I found that six of the cases that we had presented on, 48, six out the 48, were of what I would say is a relevant age, they were less than 6 weeks old and they were probably directly relevant to this case -- or the most relevant.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: In those cases -- because of course one of the points you have made is that air in the great vessels without an explanation is very rare.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: That's the gist of the evidence you have given.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: In those cases were there objectively reasons for air being in the great vessels (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In the six cases that I found -- most importantly I think I only found gas in the great vessels and in two of those cases and in both of those case there was an explanation.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And what was the explanation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: One was a baby who died with a twist in the small bowel, so a clear explanation as to why there would be gas in the great vessels near the bowel, and in another baby who was premature they had died of necrotising enterocolitis and infection. So -- and that baby had a very, very small locule of gas in the IVC, so the significance of it being very small is that's the sort of thing that you wouldn't see on an X-ray.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In only two of those cases of the six where they would be relevant, out of the 50 or so in the paper, there were no unexplained cases of post-mortem gas in the great vessels.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. And even in the explained cases, was the amount of gas that was found comparable to the amounts of gas that were found in the cases of [Baby A] and [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, not directly comparable. So the one where they died of NEC had a very small locule of gas and a bubble, effectively. The other one, who died of bowel twisting, had quite a lot of gas throughout the system, as you might expect with that sort of abnormality.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Just to bring back to mind the images that you were referring to when you gave this evidence originally, were they both pictures taken from the side of the child?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The CT scan is a picture taken all the way round --
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Sorry, I'm talking about the radiographs that we were looking at --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: -- on the occasion that you gave this evidence.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So these were the images from the side with the line of bubbles, in effect, lying above the spine?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I'm sure we can all bring that back to mind.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I'm sure you'll remember the X-ray in question, but if necessary it can be put up again if anyone wants.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It can be if anybody wants to see it. They were fairly similar pictures?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Just to bring it back to mind, I think you told us that when we dealt with [Baby E], there was a case about to come where there was more --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: -- and that was [Baby D]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Sorry, not [Baby E], [Baby A].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My fault, sorry. I made the mistake because I was about to go to [Baby E].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: So can we turn then, please, Professor Arthurs, to the case of [Baby E].
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Just to remind the jury, this is count 5. If I can just put this into -- bring him back to mind specifically.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'm looking at your statement dated 19 May 2020. There you record [Baby E]'s details in summary, that he was born on 29 July 2015, his gestation at birth was 29 weeks and 5 days, his birth weight, 1,327 grams --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: -- and that he died on 4 August 2015 at 01.40. Just to remind the jury, my Lord, this is the case where [Mother of Babies E & F], his mother, gave evidence. She told the jury that she'd seen blood on his mouth at 9 pm, 21.00 hours, on 3 August. And Lucy Letby was looking after him and she -- the phone calls between [Mother of Babies E & F] and her husband or a phone call calling him in, that evidence.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Do you remember that case with the phone calls, and from the telephone data she was able to say when the call was made? It just brings it back to mind because you've heard a lot of evidence since then. But thank you, that's the context.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's the context.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Professor Arthurs, going to your report, and the other detail that I would like to remind the jury of, my Lord, is there wasn't a post-mortem examination in this case.
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You were given a deal of material, weren't you, professor, so far as [Baby E]' case was concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: That included statements from Dr Evans dated 31 May 2018 and 24 March 2019, and a report from Dr Marnerides, the pathologist, dated 23 January 2019; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You also received two X-rays or radiographs of [Baby E]?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: I'd like to deal with one of those if we may, reminding ourselves, if we can, that [Baby E] was born at 17.53 on Wednesday, 29 July 2015. The first radiograph you received was dated 30 July 2015 at 10.41; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The second, which I invite Mr Murphy to put up from the [Baby E] sequence -- and it is tile 161 in the [Baby E] sequence -- is a radiograph dated 4 August 2015 at 00.27.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So this image, just to put it into the chronology, is taken in life, taken about 9 minutes before CPR was started on [Baby E] and taken about an hour and 15 minutes or so before he died.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can you help us, please, Dr Arthurs, with this -- and just for the sake of your Lordship and anyone else's notes, I'm going to section 5 of Professor Arthurs' report and, in particular, paragraph 4 of section 5.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Can you talk us through --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, absolutely. So this is clearly a small baby as their entire chest and abdomen fits, if you like, on one image. So this is the top (indicating) and you can see an endotracheal tube -- I don't know if you can see my arrow on there. There's an endotracheal tube, so that is in place to help ventilate the baby.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The black aspects both sides of here are the lungs and you can see the ribs either side. So the lungs are clear, there's nothing abnormal in the lungs at that stage.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: The big white blob in the middle is the heart. Then going further down, there is this white patch, the liver, and then bowel gas in the rest of the abdomen.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: In fact, they still have the umbilical clip on, which you can see just crossing there in the abdomen (indicating).
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So this is effectively a normal image of a normal baby on the unit. So the lungs are clear, none of the bowel gas is dilated, there's the normal heart and liver. You can't see the stomach on this, but there's no significance to that. So this is effectively a normal picture.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. Does the fact that you can't see the stomach inform the issue of whether or not there was air in the stomach?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, a small amount of air, you would see it. You can see there's a nasogastric tube in, and I actually make the comment that this isn't a particularly good radiograph, you can't really discriminate the grey and white things as easily as we will in subsequent radiographs.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: If we can zoom in. Can you see there's a faint line that crosses down the chest and goes to the right of the image, the left of the baby, here? So that would be a nasogastric tube and the stomach bubble would be here (indicating) if there was air in it.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes, if. No one is saying there is --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: There isn't on here, but there's not a great deal of significance to that.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: No. So -- and I'm really looking now to your report written much more recently, dated 14 July 2022, which deals with all the children.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Did you conclude that there were in reality no significant abnormalities in this radiograph?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: If it were to be suggested that if it was an air embolus, air in the circulation, that killed [Baby E], that we'd be able to see that in the radiograph, what would you say?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: First of all, we don't see that on the radiograph. But there would have to be quite a lot of air for you to see it on the radiograph and that would have to have been done quite close
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: in time, so the radiograph would have to have been taken almost immediately were that to have happened.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I can't exclude the fact that that may have happened, but it's just not demonstrated on the X-ray.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So does it follow that the fact that one can't see air in the great vessels or other parts of the circulation on this, that fact doesn't help either way in determining whether that was the cause of death?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, and that's my conclusion: I don't think this contributes either way.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: No, thank you.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: What about the issue of NEC? Does the radiograph help with determining whether or not [Baby E] had NEC?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Only insofar as there are no features of necrotising enterocolitis on the X-ray. If the baby were to die of NEC within hours of the X-ray, you might expect to see some of those features.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes. So insofar as this image assists with that question, it does not support any suggestion that this is a case of NEC?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm going to turn to [Baby F] next, please, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: His case is count 6. [Baby F], of course, was born at the same time or a minute later than his twin, [Baby E], on 29 July. The allegation concerning [Baby F] is one of attempted murder. The issue, the factual issue, for the jury revolves around the TPN bag that was connected to [Baby F] at 00.25 on 5 August. In other words, the day after, almost exactly 24 hours after, his twin [Baby E] died. The allegation centres around the issue of who it was that put insulin into the TPN bag.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Professor Arthurs, you wrote a report in [Baby F]'s case, dated 21 January 2020; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You were given, as in other cases, Dr Evans' reports that existed as at that time?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: You also received Dr Bohin's report, dated 4 April 2019?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And you were given four separate radiographs, two from 29 July, one from the 30th and the final one timed at 11.41 hours on 5 August?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So putting that into the factual matrix, about 11.5 hours after the -- 11 hours and 20 minutes or so after the TPN bag was connected to [Baby F], give or take.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Now, is there any assistance that you can provide from the radiographs that you have seen that helps at all with the issue of, first, whether there was insulin in the bag and, two, who it was that put it there?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: In short, no. They are not things that can be seen on X-ray images, but none of [Baby F]'s X-rays were done because they were worried about his heart or lungs or anything. And in fact, the last radiograph was done to look at where his long line was.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So as far as I can see, I can make no comment on those.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we turn next, please, to the case of [Baby G].
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: My Lord, the count concerning [Baby G] is count 7. Just to remind us all, [Baby G]'s birth was 31 May 2015. She was born at Arrowe Park. She was transferred to Chester on 13 August 2015. There are two incidents relating to [Baby G]. They are two allegations of attempted murder, the first on 7 September and the second on 21 September.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: This is evidence that the jury has heard more recently.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They will recall, I'm sure, the first incident concerned a projectile vomit, for which we have a picture which has been annotated by Ailsa Simpson. The issue was the withdrawal or the aspiration of 45ml of milk from [Baby G]'s stomach after the
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: vomit, set against the record that established that she had been fed 45ml.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So let's deal with that event first, Professor Arthurs. Is your initial report on [Baby G]'s case dated 19 May 2020?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: As before, were you sent two statements of Dr Evans, dated 31 May 2018 and 24 March 2019?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: A report from Dr Bohin dated 28 March 2019?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And also in [Baby G]'s case, quite a lot of radiographs?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Dealing with the relevant radiographs first of all, and dealing with the first collapse first, so the collapse of 7 September, did you receive the following radiographs taken on that day? One at 4.49 hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: For anyone's note, that's at T96. The second at 6.36 hours?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And again, for anyone's note, that's T127. These are both in the [Baby G] sequence, I should have said.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And the third, also in the [Baby G] 1 sequence, tile 205.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: You have annotated these radiographs, haven't you, professor?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I have, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: And what I'd like to do now is to produce, show to the jury and exhibit those annotated radiographs. If Mr Murphy can help us with this, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Let's take this slowly. This is a radiograph from Arrowe Park, actually, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, it doesn't pertain to the dates you just mentioned.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: No. But just for reference, it features in your report and it may be a good introduction to the issues we're going to be looking at. What does it show us? Can we deal with the -- the date and time in the top left corner is superimposed on the picture itself, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's my annotation but it's based on the image that I was provided with. You should disregard these white lines that go across the radiographs. They are ECG dots on the outside of the baby.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So they are not on the inside, so they are clear to see on the outside, so that's not the reason the X-ray is being taken.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They show a nasogastric tube in here, going into the stomach. The stomach, like the other babies, is not dilated. There is oxygen tubing, again outside of the patient, going across the top, which again is largely irrelevant to the image. And then they show lots of dilated loops of bowel. This particular loop is dilated more than the others (indicating).
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: What about the two arrows that we see that you've put on?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The arrows here denote the nasogastric tube, just to make it clear to people what the normal passage down the oesophagus and into the left-hand side of the baby into the stomach is.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So that's a reference for us?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Can we move on to the next radiograph in your report, please. This is still pre either of the incidents that we are concerned with. Does this also originate from Arrowe Park?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: What does it show, please?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Again, much the same. There is a nasogastric tube in.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: It has gone a little bit further. These are the overlapping -the white lines are the overlapping ECG probes outside of the patient. But it just shows again normal sort of bowel gas, a few bowel loops of which are dilated.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Thank you. The next radiograph, please? This is now one from Chester, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct, that's 7 September, yes.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Just to put this into the chronology, my Lord, this is some time between 2 and 2.5 hours after the incident, after the projectile vomiting.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So what do we see here?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Similarly, I've labelled the nasogastric tube that can be seen. Lots of loops of bowel. Most of this is small bowel. There might be a loop of large bowel which I've written "LB" over there. The stomach is not dilated.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Presumably if there's been a large vomit then that would account for the stomach being decompressed. And she's beginning now to develop complications of lung disease of prematurity. So the lungs are not as black as they would be otherwise.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Just to cross-reference this image to the sequence of events, the unannotated version of this appears in the [Baby G] 1 sequence of events at T96. Can we move to the next radiograph, please, which is taken almost 2 hours later at 06.36. Sorry, no, that's the wrong one.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I don't think I have that in the --
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: Right, okay. That doesn't matter. The one we saw is the first radiograph taken after the incident, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's right.
blocks.speaker: ARTHURS

blocks.text: So if we could just go back to it, please, sorry. This is 7 September?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: body, you'd expect it to go down the channel it was put in, but also to spread?

blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: Okay. Did anyone else attend during the course of the resuscitation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Not that I can recall.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Do you remember whether [Baby I]'s parents were present at any stage?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Sorry, yes.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Are you able to help us with what stage they arrived?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, I've never been able to truly remember. It's only ever come from the nursing notes and things like that.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Did you speak to them at all?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I must have because I directed them to call them --
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: -- and I recall, in my mind, [Baby I]'s mum touching [Baby I] as we were trying to revive her.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Okay. We know that there came a point where the resuscitation came to an end.
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Whose decision was that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Gibbs'.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Why was that?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Because we'd worked for a period of time and there'd been no sign of improvement at all.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Once that decision was made, do you recall what happened?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: To who?
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Well, to [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: At that point, I left.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Okay. So you were there for the attempts at resuscitation?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Once they sadly had failed --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: -- you left?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: And presumably other patients required --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. I stayed on the unit for a while, as long as I could, until -- I will have been called away again.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Did you attend a debrief after the (overspeaking) --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: I didn't attend one, no.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Have you reflected on the death of [Baby I] --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: -- and the causes?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: And the shift generally?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: And what has that caused you, if anything, to think?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Just that I've never been able to truly explain it, that it was awful. But I was never worried, I knew we'd done everything, and I'd done everything the way I did it the first time I attended and I trusted everyone around me implicitly.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Okay. Thank you, doctor, I have no more questions for you. If you could wait there, please.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS

Just one thing, Dr Chang. It sounds quite small after the enormity of what you've been describing to us, but I did want to ask about this. You told us there was a discussion between you and Dr Gibbs about whether to extubate or not --
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: -- in between the two incidents. When you were asked questions, you said there were pros and cons with both.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: And one of the pros was that if you take her off the ventilator then you wouldn't have to sedate or paralyse her because of how she'd been fighting the ventilator?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: What were the cons in taking her off the ventilator?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can I have a minute just to think?
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: (Pause)

In the clinical scenario that we faced, there were minimal cons. On reflection, the cons are that if she had been on a ventilator, she would have been breathing, someone would have been assisting with her breathing, but that's it. The benefits overweighed them so much, because we made that decision.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: For those of us who don't have to make these decisions and don't deal with this, we know from what you have put in the notes on the first part of the incident that there had been a cardiac arrest and she required resuscitation --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: -- and -- were you aware of her clinical history at the time you were dealing with this?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: From what you can recall, was that all taken into account when weighing up the pros and cons?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: All right. That's what I wanted to check, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR ASTBURY
When later ventilated, did that assist with [Baby I]'s saturations? When you were forced to ventilate her at 1 o'clock in the morning, did that assist?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: No, no, no.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Does my Lord have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I don't, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Chang won't be required again?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: No, we don't expect Dr Chang back again.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you very much for being available today and giving evidence. I know that you were yesterday as well.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes, thank you so much.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: I'm sorry you've been inconvenienced to that extra extent. Thank you very much. It's not expected that you're going to be required to give evidence about anything else to do
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: with this case, but just in case, would you please not talk to anyone about anything to do with this case --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Of course.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: -- any of the patients? I'm saying this to everyone in your situation, just in case someone decides that you are for some reason, unforeseen at the moment, asked to come back --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Of course. Thank you so much.
blocks.speaker: CHANG

blocks.text: Until it's all over. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
I think we don't have any more witnesses to give oral evidence, but there are some statements that can be read?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: There are, yes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: So we'll have a break. Can you give us an estimate as to how long the statements are likely to take?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: About 15 minutes, I think.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: I still think we'll have a break. I think we should have a short break. No more than 10 minutes, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

Witness statement of MS CAROLINE OAKLEY (read)
My Lord, I'm going to return to the statement, first, please, of Caroline Oakley, part of it. It is page 68 of my Lord's bundle. We've heard part of it in an earlier part, dated 6 April 2018.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Following on, ladies and gentlemen, in her statement, Caroline Oakley says this:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The second date that I have been asked about is the 22nd into 23 October 2015, the day when [Baby I] died.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was on a day shift on 22 October, starting at 07.30 hours, so was not there when she passed away, but I was her designated nurse during that day.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been able to review my notes and it looks like she had a good day on the day shift. I basically put that she had a long line in, fluids going through, and she was nil by mouth, waiting to go to Alder Hey for a barium enema.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She was unsettled at time, obviously very hungry, but usually settled with a dummy. We were getting minimal clear aspirates from her NG tube and her abdomen was fine, soft and not distended. She'd also weed and pooed and her cares were attended to by mum.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I do sort of remember that time with her because I remember her mum getting frustrated about this appointment at Alder Hey and me trying to chase the doctors and nagging them to try to get the appointment sorted. Because she'd had so many episodes of her tummy blowing up, I think they must have decided to keep her nil by mouth until she had this test done. Mum and dad were really angry with Alder Hey because it hadn't been sorted. If I recall, I was told that the post-mortem didn't show anything, so that would indicate that the barium wouldn't have helped, but you don't know that at the time.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I just remember her being a lovely, beautiful but problematic baby. She was a bit older, so she was more responsive, like eye contact and things.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember her because of the investigations that weren't done, ie the barium enema, because that was upsetting, seeing her lying there stuck in a cot, awake and hungry.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I had come to a day shift again on 23 October and I remember the bereavement part a little because the cold mattress that we nursed babies on when they died kept heating up and alarming. At times like that you want everything to run smoothly, not being made to look incompetent by a piece of equipment.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I don't remember anything else about that day other than [Baby I] being with her family in bedroom 2. I basically would have left her with her parents and then be doing the bereavement paperwork. The night staff had already done the memory box.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dr Gibbs spoke to mum and dad and told them the coroner wanted a post-mortem. They weren't happy but understood it was a legal requirement. Because they weren't happy with Alder Hey, they didn't want [Baby I] staying there after the post-mortem.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The bereavement coordinator, whose name I can't recall, was involved and spoke with Alder Hey who said they would facilitate getting [Baby I] back to the Countess after the post-mortem. The medical photographer came and took some lovely photos for mum and dad. I can't remember her name.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "From my notes, [Baby I] then went to the mortuary at approximately 2 pm. I then escorted mum and dad to the mortuary at 3 pm for their appointment to see her. They must have come back to the unit to collect all the mementos as my notes reflect this.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "They also reflect that the parents had another appointment at the mortuary the next day to go back and see [Baby I]."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of DR BHUVANESHWARI LADDE (read)
The next statement, please, my Lord, is in the fourth bundle, back to the fourth bundle, at page 93.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: In a statement dated 8 June 2020, Bhuvaneshwari Ladde states:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My name is Bhuvaneshwari Ladde, I am currently a general practitioner. I was working as a general practice specialist trainee year 1 in paediatrics at the Countess of Chester Hospital NHS Trust between 5 August 2015 to 2 February 2016. I have been asked by Cheshire Police to provide a witness statement in relation to my involvement with one patient, [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My statement is solely based on reviewing the medical records. According to the clinical records, I had documented notes on three occasions.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "(1) I documented notes following a consultant-led head grand round by Dr Brearey on 2 September 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "(2) I reviewed bloods on 4 September 2015 and discussed the results with the neonatal registrar, Dr Matt, and actioned the results as per his advice.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "And (3) in the early hours of 23 October 2015, I was on duty as GPS ST1 paediatrics SHO rota at the Countess of Chester Hospital when an emergency resus call was put out for [Baby I], requiring emergency medical assistance.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I can't recall that event at all. I cannot recall who was present and the statement is purely based on the medical notes that I have reviewed. My role in this resuscitation was limited to documenting the drugs that were given during the resuscitation. I was not involved in decision-making about the
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: drugs or the doses of the medications. I was not involved in decision-making about [he repeats the same line] the drugs or the doses of the medications. I was also not the person who administered the drugs. I have noted that medications had been retrospectively documented on the electronic system after resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "From the medical notes and identifying my own handwriting, I have recorded the list of drugs given to [Baby I] during her resuscitation."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: If I can just ask, rather than read it, my Lord, to put tile 142 up. In his statement, Dr Ladde simply lists what's shown on his original document. Then he states -- just to complete -- thank you. Everyone's seen it.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Dr Ladde goes on:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "'Flush' in the notes indicates sodium chloride, 0.9%, which is used to flush the line after the medication administration. In addition, the asterisk that I put at 01.43 and 02.00 against two doses is because of the different strength of adrenaline used here (1 in 1,000) which was as per consultant paediatrician Dr Gibbs' decision, who was the resuscitation lead.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The list of medication is included in [Baby I]'s medical notes and was subsequently signed by myself. Reading from the medical notes, this was my only contribution to the event."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of CHRISTOPHER BOOTH (read)
Moving on, please, my Lord, to Christopher Booth, page 97. He states in a statement dated 16 May 2018:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked by DC Birch of the Cheshire Police about my recollections and knowledge of a baby called [Baby I] and the night she died on 23 October 2015. I have had the opportunity to review the notes of that night, but I also have my own recollections.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "[Baby I], from what I recall, was about 10 weeks old at the time. She was a prem baby who'd had numerous investigations into a distended abdomen. She was waiting for a barium enema, I think to be done at Alder Hey, but that was a forthcoming investigation. She was nil by mouth at the time and she had a long line in situ into a large vessel, so we could give longterm intravenous fluid, but that had to be removed that evening because it was occluding. She was in nursery 1 that evening.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She did have periods of being really quite unsettled at the time because she was not being fed and on that evening she was
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: really unsettled particularly around 11 or 12-ish. Normally, she could be placated with like a dummy or what we call containment holding where you place a hand over them to calm them down. But she was really quite fractious up to about midnight when she became apnoeic (stopped breathing).
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Her oxygen levels started to drop. Her heart rate started to drop, so resuscitation manoeuvres were undertaken by Ashleigh Hudson and the doctors were crash bleeped. I think it was Dr Chang who attended and Dr Gibbs was called in and I think [Baby I] did need full resuscitation.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I did cardiac compressions and she was intubated and ventilated. Dr Gibbs attended and I'm pretty sure she needed resuscitation drugs but the exact drugs I'm not sure of. She became very fractious and was fighting against the ventilator and sometimes when babies do that, it becomes counterproductive, so the decision was made to extubate her and so the breathing tube was taken out.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She then seemed okay for a while, she was breathing independently, looking round and rooting. I'm pretty sure Dr Gibbs left then as he was satisfied she was okay and I think as a team we felt she'd recovered from this episode.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "About an hour later, she dropped again. She lost her colour, dropped her oxygen levels and her heart rate dropped. I'm pretty sure Dr Chang was in theatre at that time at a delivery, so Lucy Letby and I managed her airway and undertook normal ABC resuscitation manoeuvres and Ashleigh ran to theatre to get Rachel Chang. Theatre is just beyond nursery 1, about 50 yards away, so it was quicker than crash bleeping her. She came through and it was full resus again.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dr Gibbs was called and he came in as he wasn't very far away. He acted as team leader. The senior doctors took charge of the resus. Ashleigh took charge of cardiac compressions, I think, and I think myself and Mel Taylor were drawing up drugs; it needs two registered nurses to do that. Lots of adrenaline was given and there were episodes where her heart rate rose and we thought we had her back, then it would drop again.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The parents had been called in and it goes without saying it was very, very distressing for them to watch their daughter being resuscitated.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was very dire indeed and it became apparent there was pulseless activity. She maintained her heart rate on the monitor, but it wasn't strong enough to produce a pulse. It was fruitless, really, and we were getting nowhere. So the decision was made, with the parents' consent, at about 2 am to withdraw
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: resuscitation attempts. So she was wrapped in a blanket and Ashleigh handed her to mum and dad and she was pronounced dead at about 2.30 am.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "It was particularly upsetting because in that 10 weeks we'd got to know the family really well and got to know [Baby I] really well because she was quite a character herself and we were all very fond of her and had high hopes for her. So I think everyone was extremely upset. We'd all looked after her a lot and got to know the family. It was gut-wrenching for the team as a group. I wrote an email to the ward manager, Eirian Powell, that morning as we were all heartbroken. I wanted to convey to her how hard the team had worked and how upset they were.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I wanted her to know that as a team everyone had tried their hardest and did their bit. The team I work with are an amazing team, particularly at that time. If we weren't such a good team we would have crumbled as there were so many horrible things going on, but we just supported each other.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked if on that night I was designated nurse for any baby but I honestly can't remember.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The drugs given to [Baby I] that night were from the resus trolley and I'm pretty sure we exhausted those supplies and had to break into the two separate resus boxes from pharmacy because we were going through a lot of adrenaline.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I believe there was a debrief a couple of weeks after [Baby I]'s death, which was led by Dr Gibbs. At this time I can't think of anything else that may assist the investigation."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS MELANIE TAYLOR (read)
My Lord, next, please, page 100, which is Melanie Taylor and a statement dated 1 October 2018.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: She says:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been asked by DC Birch from Cheshire Police about my involvement in the care of a baby called [Baby I] in 2015 at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The first date I was asked about was 30 September 2015. I had the opportunity prior to seeing DC Birch of reviewing the nursing notes for that date. I was on a long day that day. I remember [Baby I] very well because she was on the unit for a long time and she had quite a few problems that meant she was transferred off the unit a few times.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "it's the type of environment where you get to know the patients and parents very well and I know she had had episodes where she'd needed resuscitation. But my honest recollections are that I don't really remember the date of 30 September much at all.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The notes say I rang the parents and I do vaguely remember calling them, thinking this may be a very serious situation, but that's all I genuinely recall. I wasn't looking after her personally and wasn't directly involved in what was going on.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I think [Baby I] was the second baby whose death I was directly involved with on the unit and before that I was there a few years and wasn't involved in another death. I was never concerned about any of the care or treatment that the babies had on the unit.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have also been asked about the 22nd into 23 October 2015 by DC Birch. This was the night that [Baby I], sadly, died. Again, I have had the opportunity to review the notes for that night. I was on a night shift and, having looked at the notes, I can say Ashleigh Hudson was on and was looking after [Baby I]. Chris Booth has said he was on that night, but I can only vaguely recall him. I think Val Thomas was on too. I don't really remember the doctors who were on, but I know from the notes Dr Gibbs and Dr Rachel Chang were there.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I don't remember a great deal about the actual shift that night. I can't remember where I was or anything about when the call for assistance came. I can't remember which baby I was looking after or in which nursery.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I think with regard to [Baby I]'s resuscitation, I was involved in drawing up drugs, ie adrenaline, and wasn't doing CPR; that was Ashleigh and someone else. What I remember more from the shift is more the emotional side, seeing her parents come in, trying to talk to them and seeing their reaction. And after [Baby I] died I just remember how upset her parents were.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have memories of leaving them behind screens with her. For me, my memories of that night are more about the parents, but also my own emotions because obviously we were all devastated, even more so because we knew the family and [Baby I] so well and they'd been through so much. It was just pure shock.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She was stable before that. She had had episodes before that and was in and out of the hospital, when she'd dip and get transferred to one of the bigger hospitals, then she'd get well and come back.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I think her parents came in during the resuscitation but I don't know who called them. I don't even know if it was me.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I remember them walking into nursery 1 and standing there, not really knowing what to do, and myself personally not really knowing what to say. Generally, someone in the peripheral area will take the lead and be responsible to speak to them, maybe someone drawing up drugs or making notes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The actual resuscitation is a bit of a blur, to be honest. I can remember right at the end when the doctor decided to call it and said we should stop. I feel like I was either administering or drawing up drugs and was just shocked when he said stop. Everyone has their role to play and there's usually lots of people in the room. I had been looking at [Baby I] and then the monitor thinking she was going to come out of it and then when she didn't, my heart just dropped. When he said stop I was just devastated, especially when I looked at her parents.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "As far as the bereavement paperwork went, I think that may have been down to the person responsible for [Baby I] form the next shift as it was nearer the end of the shift. We let the parents spend a lot of time with their baby and it would be down to the designated nurse to help with the memory box. I want to say that Lucy Letby helped a lot with that, but the paperwork side of it was probably down to the next shift.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I think Lucy was on a couple of other shifts I was on where babies had died and she was quite involved with doing memory boxes on those occasions so she was used to doing them. The memory boxes are from a charity set up by someone who lost a baby called 4Louis. We do handprints and footprint and take a lock of hair. It's about what the parents want to do.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We offer parents the use of our unit camera and each box has a memory card in so that they can keep the photos. We keep a stock of these boxes and Jo Williams and myself are responsible for ordering these from the charity. We get them directly from the 4Louis website. Jo and I cascade a bit of training to other staff about how to use them through the bereavement packs we put together for them. The packs also contain the paperwork and how to complete it.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In conclusion, I can't think of any other information that I can offer at this stage that may assist the investigation into [Baby I]'s death."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS VALERIE THOMAS (read)
My Lord, finally this afternoon, the statement of Valerie Thomas, a statement dated 18 September 2018.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: At 105 in my Lord's bundle. Valerie Thomas says:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I started training in January 1975 and qualified as a nurse in December 1977. I started work on the maternity wing at the Countess of Chester Hospital in June 1978 and have worked there ever since.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "As regards to qualifications, I am a band 4 nurse. I have been asked by DC Birch of Cheshire Police about a baby called [Baby I] and my involvement with her and my recollections of her from 2015. I have had the opportunity to review the nursing notes for [Baby I] prior to making this statement.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My first recollections of [Baby I] were from 5 September 2015. I had come on nights that night and was allocated [Baby I] to care for. I had received a handover and at that point I think she had started to not be quite right. She was starting to desaturate.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Within an hour of me being on, she had desatted up and down and it was decided to pass her over to more qualified staff. I passed her over to [Nurse C] and she passed her on to Yvonne Griffiths later than night. Both of them are band 6s.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She had obviously been well to be allocated to me. At my level we don't take any really poorly babies and she'd been well enough to work through the nurseries. I can't remember exactly where she was but she wasn't in nursery 1 that night.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was a nurse the night before on 4 September. I have had the chance to go through the notes I wrote for that night and it did jog my memory. I was her designated nurse and [Baby I] was breathing for herself and her temperature was stable. My notes show she was having expressed breast milk every 3 hours via her nasogastric tube and we were looking for mum to offer her the first bottle.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She wouldn't have been in nursery 4 as she was still in an incubator, so she would have been in 2 or 3. Nothing in the notes says it was anything other than an uneventful night. I finished at 8 am on 5 September and then back on duty 7.30 that night.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I'd have received a full handover that night, but I can't recall anything other than that she was starting to desaturate. Nothing stands out. [Nurse C]'s notes state that [Baby I] continued to desaturate and needed ventilator support. I can't remember what support she had as she was moved into nursery 1 and my involvement ceased.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have also been asked by DC Birch about 30 September 2015. I have been able to review the nursing notes for that night prior
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: to making the statement. I can't remember anything about [Baby I]'s handover and have no knowledge of her care that night. I now know from the notes it was Lucy Letby handing over to Bernie Butterworth but I have no recollection or personal knowledge at all about that.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Finally, I have been asked about the night of 22 October into the 23 October 2015, which was the night that [Baby I] died. Again, I have had the opportunity to review the nursing notes made that night prior to making this statement.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Again, I was on a night shift, I had a baby on transition care that night, and I think it was my first night back after annual leave.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I only had one baby up on the ward and would have been allocated babies on the unit downstairs. I wouldn't have spent too much time on transitional care but I can recollect that I had been up on the transitional care ward at one point and came down to the unit. The phone was ringing but no one was at the desk. I answered it and it was [Baby I]'s mum.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At that stage I didn't realise what was going on in nursery 1 as I had been upstairs. I subsequently found out it was [Baby I] who was very poorly. When I answered the phone, [Baby I]'s mum knew that [Baby I] wasn't well, so she must have been spoken to earlier and was ringing back to see how she was.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I went into nursery 1 and said that [Baby I]'s mum was on the phone, not realising that [Baby I] was being resuscitated in there. Lucy Letby said that [Baby I]'s parents should come in.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I then waited for her mum and dad to come in by the door to let them in. I didn't get involved in any of the resuscitation at all. By that time there was Ashleigh Hudson, Lucy Letby, Chris Booth and two doctors. I might have taken a call from Dr Gibbs, who was asking what the problem was. I think I just said, 'It's [Baby I], you need to come in', but other than that, my involvement was minimal.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was not aware that [Baby I] had suffered an earlier collapse that night around midnight. When I went into nursery 1, having taken the call from [Baby I]'s mum, I think it was Lucy and Ashleigh doing the CPR, but I can't recall who else was doing what. There's nothing else that sticks in my memory from that night other than I think I stayed down on the unit to help look after all the other babies while the rest of the staff were busy with [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I don't remember there being any conversation amongst the staff after [Baby I] had died. It goes very quiet after something like
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: that. There is usually a debrief process after a baby dies, but I have never been on one. It wasn't a compulsory attendance thing, but I think that may now have changed.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In conclusion, I would like to say it was a busy time on the unit, but shifts were covered and I had no concerns about anything or anyone on the unit. A lot of the babies were very poorly and had very complex needs, but everyone did their best."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That concludes those statements, my Lord.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: Thank you very much. Well, the next witness will be Dr Gibbs --

No research, no communication with anyone about anything about to do with this case. 10.30 on Monday morning, please. Thank you.
